segments.en: Talofa! That is how people say hello in Tuvalu, a scattering of tiny islands in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, halfway between Hawaii and Australia.

Tuvalu is made of nine small islands, some of them ring-shaped atolls wrapped around bright blue lagoons. The land is so low and narrow that from the middle of an island you can often hear the ocean on both sides.

The main atoll is Funafuti, home to the capital. Its airstrip is one of the few big open spaces, so in the cool of the evening, when no plane is due, it becomes a playground for football, volleyball and families out for a stroll.
Life here moves gently. Houses are open to the breeze, bicycles and scooters hum along the single main road, and neighbours know one another by name.
Each island has a maneapa, a large community meeting house with a high roof and open sides. This is where elders gather to make decisions, and where feasts, dances and celebrations take place.
If you are invited to a feast, you will sit on woven mats on the floor. Food is shared generously, and it is polite to eat a little of everything and to thank your hosts warmly.

The ocean feeds everyone. Fish is caught fresh from the lagoon and the open sea, and it is often eaten with pulaka, a starchy root grown in pits dug deep into the island, along with coconut, breadfruit and banana.
Coconut palms are precious. Their nuts give fresh water to drink and cream for cooking, and their leaves are woven into mats, baskets and fans.
The fatele is Tuvalu's favourite dance. It starts slowly, with singers seated around a wooden box that is beaten like a drum, then grows faster and louder until everyone is laughing and clapping.
People here speak Tuvaluan, a Polynesian language, as well as English. Faith is important to many families, and Sunday is a quiet day of church, hymns and rest.
Because the islands rise only a few metres above the sea, Tuvaluans speak up around the world about protecting the ocean and the climate. Their voice is small, but it is heard.
Before you leave, take a moment on the lagoon shore at sunset, when the water turns gold and pink and children splash in the shallows.
Then set your course across the open blue to the south, where the islands of Fiji are waiting with a big bula welcome.
